terminal_record.title: Trump Opposed Postal Funding While Linking It to Mail Voting
terminal_record.description_short: Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding in August 2020 and said it was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting.
terminal_record.description_medium: In August 2020, Donald Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding during COVID-19 relief negotiations and said the money was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting. CNBC reported the remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy rejecting the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction. The reporting does not substantiate the original claim that Trump pressured DeJoy to slow delivery.
terminal_record.description_long: On August 13, 2020, President Donald Trump opposed additional funding for the U.S. Postal Service during negotiations over coronavirus relief. In a Fox Business interview, he said the Postal Service needed money to process “all of these millions and millions of ballots” and said that without a deal it could not have universal mail-in voting. CNBC reported those remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy saying the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction was “wholly off-base.” The reporting supports Trump’s public funding position and the connection he expressly made between postal resources and mail voting. It does not establish that Trump personally directed DeJoy to slow mail delivery. The supplied research notes also distinguish Trump’s opposition to funding from DeJoy’s separate operational changes and report that Trump said he did not know what DeJoy was doing. This record should describe the funding dispute and statement, not assert an unproven instruction to reduce delivery service, voter-suppression intent, or resulting postal harm. No enacted funding decision or measured effect is established by the cited article.
terminal_record.date_precision: day; CNBC publication date and interview remarks are August 13, 2020.
terminal_record.subcategory: Postal Service funding and mail voting

terminal_record.title: Federal task force sends Columbia nine preconditions for funding negotiations
terminal_record.description_short: A federal task force's March 13 letter set nine preconditions for formal negotiations over restoring Columbia University's canceled federal grants and contracts.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 13, 2025, the federal Joint Task Force to Combat Antisemitism sent Columbia University a letter listing nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts, according to a March 24 release by HHS, Education and GSA. This repair covers the later letter only. It excludes the March 7 cancellation, already proposed as a separate event in supplied entry-5752, and does not retain unsupported claims of threats of criminal prosecution.
terminal_record.description_long: On March 13, 2025, the federal Joint Task Force to Combat Antisemitism sent Columbia University a letter setting out nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts, according to a March 24 joint release by HHS, Education and GSA. The government statement said Columbia committed to changes involving admissions review, protest and masking rules, immigration-law compliance, regional-studies programs beginning with Middle East and Israel, discipline for Hamilton Hall and encampment cases, the structure of its judicial board, campus security powers, and its Tel Aviv center. This card describes the letter's stated terms and the administration's use of funding restoration as leverage. It does not claim that every requested change was implemented, that the conditions had legal force beyond the funding relationship, or that criminal prosecution was threatened as part of this letter; the frozen entry's prosecution claim is not supported by the reviewed source. The March 7 announcement canceling about $400 million is a separately dated event already proposed in supplied entry-5752, so it is excluded here to avoid duplicate event coverage.
terminal_record.date_precision: Specific date stated in the March 24 GSA release.

source_fact_map.fact: The March 13 letter set nine preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts.
source_fact_map.quote: March 13th letter detailing 9 preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Today, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Education (ED), and the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) welcomed the statement by Columbia University outlining actions the university is taking in response to the Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism’s March 13th letter detailing 9 preconditions for formal negotiations to restore canceled federal grants and contracts.

source_fact_map.fact: The list of Columbia commitments included review of regional-studies programs beginning with Middle East and Israel.
source_fact_map.quote: Reviewing the portfolio of regional studies programs, starting immediately with those that teach about the Middle East and Israel.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
Columbia has committed to:

- Reviewing admissions procedures to ensure an unbiased admissions process and specifically studying the decline in admissions of Jewish students.
- Clarifying time, place, and manner restrictions to clearly state that protests in academic buildings, and other places necessary for the conduct of university activities, are unacceptable.
- Enforcing a strict anti-masking policy that includes appropriate enforcement mechanisms for violations, including removal from campus or detention for trespassing.
- Adhering to all student visa and immigration laws in cooperation with the Department of Homeland Security.
- Reviewing the portfolio of regional studies programs, starting immediately with those that teach about the Middle East and Israel.
- Enforcing existing disciplinary policies and completing disciplinary proceedings, with meaningful consequences, for Hamilton Hall and encampments.
- Placing the University Judicial Board (UJB) under the Office of the Provost and limiting panel membership to faculty and administrators only.
- Expanding the number of Columbia security personnel and granting them the ability to arrest and remove agitators who foster an unsafe or hostile work or study environment, or otherwise interfere with classroom instruction or the functioning of the university.
- Advance Columbia’s Tel Aviv Center. Programming for the Columbia Tel Aviv Global Hub will launch in Q2 2025.
